sources.source: Disaggregated state in Flink 2.0 (Mei et al., 2025 VLDB)

items.item: Flink 2.0 introduces an asynchronous record execution framework and a disaggregated state store, ForSt, with an LSM-tree abstraction unifying local and remote state access

at.step: Reveal: ForSt is an LSM-tree store built on remote storage

items.item: the asynchronous model preserves Flink 1.x's per-key processing order, watermark correctness, and fault tolerance guarantees

at.step: Reveal: same-key order is preserved while different keys interleave freely

items.item: checkpointing becomes a lightweight metadata update, consistently completing within a few seconds regardless of checkpoint size

at.step: Reveal: a checkpoint becomes a near-metadata update

items.item: compared to Flink 1.20, disaggregated state provides sixteen-times faster job recovery, twelve-times faster scale-in, and forty-nine-times faster scale-out

at.step: Reveal: faster recovery, scale-in, and scale-out follow from the same cause

items.item: enabling disaggregated state without any cache degrades throughput by 48% on average for heavy-I/O queries, while even a 1GB cache outperforms the local setup

at.step: Reveal: no cache costs real throughput; a modest one earns it back

items.item: ForStStateBackend is an LSM-tree structured key-value store built on top of RocksDB, holding sst files on remote file systems such as HDFS or S3

at.step: Reveal: ForSt is an LSM-tree store built on remote storage

items.item: asynchronous state access is preferred, since ForStStateBackend is currently the only backend supporting it

at.step: Reveal: the async state API returns a non-blocking future

sources.source: Working with State V2 (Apache Flink, 2.0 docs)

items.item: the new state API gives synchronous and asynchronous versions of each state type, with the asynchronous version returning a non-blocking StateFuture

at.step: Reveal: the async state API returns a non-blocking future

items.item: the new API set is only available on a KeyedStream with enableAsyncState() invoked

at.step: Reveal: the async state API returns a non-blocking future

items.item: ForSt's move is best understood as an inversion, not an addition: every earlier backend's local copy was authoritative with the remote copy (if any) derived from it; ForSt flips which side is derived, and almost every other consequence in this topic follows from that one flip.

at.step: Reveal: ForSt is an LSM-tree store built on remote storage

items.item: A checkpoint becoming near-metadata-only is not a separate optimization bolted onto ForSt — it's the direct, mechanical consequence of the authoritative copy already living where a checkpoint would need to copy it to.

at.step: Reveal: a checkpoint becomes a near-metadata update

items.item: The paper's own recovery/scale-in/scale-out multiples all share one root cause (near-free checkpoints), which is why presenting them together as one reveal, rather than three separate unrelated wins, better reflects the actual architecture.

at.step: Reveal: faster recovery, scale-in, and scale-out follow from the same cause

items.item: The per-key ordering guarantee is the one property that keeps async state access from silently breaking correctness — without it, a naive async rewrite of keyed processing would be a different, much riskier change than this topic presents it as.

at.step: Reveal: same-key order is preserved while different keys interleave freely

items.item: Framing the cache tradeoff as a real cost rather than a footnote matters because it's the one place this topic explicitly says ForSt is not strictly better than RocksDB — a latency-sensitive job with a poorly cached working set is a genuinely worse fit for it.

at.step: Reveal: no cache costs real throughput; a modest one earns it back

items.item: This topic's hook (every backend so far kept its primary copy local) and the recap's close (the primary copy moved off-machine on purpose) are the same observation stated twice, first as an open question and then as the settled answer the whole reel built toward.

at.step: Hook: what if the primary copy didn't stay next to the processing?

items.item: The toy checkpoint-cost, async-ordering, throughput, and cache-latency models are deliberately simplified standalone demonstrations, not ports of ForSt's actual LSM-tree or async-runtime internals, and every figure shown is this run's own measured output, not a cited Flink benchmark.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: This topic uses the state-backend comparison and key-group rescaling unit from the previous topic directly — ForSt is introduced as a third backend alongside heap and RocksDB, not as a replacement for the rescaling mechanics those backends already share.

at.step: Setup: heap and RocksDB both keep their primary copy local

items.item: Presenting the async state API's change as a consequence of ForSt's remote primary copy, rather than an independent feature, keeps the causal chain (remote primary -> real round-trip latency -> async access needed) explicit instead of implied.

at.step: Reveal: the async state API returns a non-blocking future

items.item: This topic deliberately leaves Flink SQL's own consumption of state through dynamic tables unexplored — the runtime and state model just covered is what that SQL layer is built directly on top of, large enough to need the next topic's full treatment.
